clue.text: Narrow piece of land can produce this sum

indicators.note: can produce suggests the following letters can be worked into something new, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A geography question: what thin strip of land can you make from this little sum?
explanation.walkthrough: 'can produce' rearranges THIS SUM.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow strip joining two larger landmasses, like Panama, is the geographer's term for this.

clue.text: Business men mostly after fashionable profits

indicators.note: after places the business pieces behind the fashionable one

parts.note: in means fashionable, as in the in thing
CO is the abbreviation for company, a business

indicators.note: mostly means most of the word, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written before shortening

explanation.surface: Businessmen chasing the latest trend for money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the last letter of 'men'; 'after' puts the business pieces behind the fashionable one. 'Business men' reads as businessmen, but splits in two.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnings or revenue received, the money coming in.

clue.text: Current sovereign at the head of one state

indicators.note: at the head of puts the first piece in front of the rest in this down entry

parts.note: sovereign means supreme or paramount, the top
one is the Roman numeral I
CAL is an abbreviation for California, a US state

explanation.surface: The reigning monarch who leads a nation today.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sovereign' is the adjective meaning supreme, not a monarch; 'at the head of' puts it in front. CAL is a US-style short form of California.
explanation.definitionFit: Topical matters are those of present interest, the affairs of the moment.

clue.text: Railway financier, they say, is needed to help with the timing

definitions.text: needed to help with the timing

parts.note: a metro is an underground city railway

indicators.note: they say means as people pronounce it, so the word is heard not spelt

parts.note: the gnomes of Zurich was a nickname for Swiss bankers

explanation.surface: A railway tycoon is said to be needed to keep the trains on schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: GNOME, as in the 'gnomes of Zurich' (Swiss bankers), sounds like NOME; 'is' links.
explanation.definitionFit: A ticking device that musicians use to keep a steady beat.

clue.text: Acrobatic feat comes to a close, holding firm for a moment

parts.note: the splits is a gymnastic move with the legs flat out in opposite directions

indicators.note: holding means containing, so one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: to end is to come to a close
CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A gymnast finishes a move holding steady for an instant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' puts the firm inside the word for coming to a close; 'for' links. 'firm' looks like an adjective about the grip, but it is a company.
explanation.definitionFit: An instant, the tiniest fraction of time.

clue.text: Snatch the sauce

explanation.surface: Grab the ketchup bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: To snatch something is to seize it up quickly; and the tomato sauce is also spelt this way, a variant of ketchup.

clue.text: Grant without a petition

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the letter is taken out

parts.note: Cary Grant was the Hollywood film star

explanation.surface: Someone granted something without having to ask.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grant' is the actor Cary Grant, so take CARY and remove A. 'Grant' looks like a verb meaning allow, but it is a surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A cry can be an urgent appeal or plea, as in a cry for help.

clue.text: An expression of disapproval — it's taken the wrong way altogether

parts.note: tut is the click of the tongue showing disapproval

indicators.note: taken the wrong way means read in the opposite direction, so the word is turned around

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Someone tuts because a remark was misunderstood by everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken the wrong way' turns IT to TI.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical direction meaning all performers together, the full orchestra playing at once.

clue.text: Greedy, like the Ettrick Shepherd?

explanation.surface: Was a famous Scottish poet a glutton?
explanation.walkthrough: The Ettrick Shepherd was the nickname of the Scottish poet James Hogg, so something like him is Hogg-ish.
explanation.definitionFit: Greedy like a pig; and, read as a pun, resembling the poet James Hogg.

clue.text: Dish that eloquence cannot improve

parts.note: alludes to the proverb that fine words butter no root vegetables, meaning fine talk achieves nothing practical

explanation.surface: A meal that no amount of fine talk can make better.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'fine words butter no parsnips' means talk alone gets nothing done.
explanation.definitionFit: A root vegetable served as a side dish, the one the proverb says flowery words cannot butter.

clue.text: To provide the finishing touch, play the last part in fine style

parts.note: to cap it all is to add the crowning finishing touch

indicators.note: the last part of a word means its final letter only

explanation.surface: An actor told to round off the evening by performing the closing scene with panache.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the last part' takes the final letter, Y, of 'play'.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned adverb meaning splendidly or excellently, as in 'he managed capitally'.

clue.text: Cat starts to thrive, in general exhibiting robustness

indicators.note: starts to points at the opening letter of each of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A cat that thrives and is generally in robust health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts to' takes the first letters of the five words from 'thrive' to 'robustness'.
explanation.definitionFit: The striped big cat of Asia is one example of the feline family.

clue.text: Computer plays a part in academic romance

indicators.note: plays a part in says the answer forms part of the words that follow, a run inside them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A computer has a role in a university love affair.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft read 'Computer plays' as the definition, but MICRO cannot mean plays; 'plays a part in' is the whole indicator and 'Computer' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A short form for a small personal machine, the microcomputer of the 1980s.

clue.text: Mastermind supply of food to artist, by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it says the pieces are to be heard spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: tack is an old word for food, as in hard tack eaten by sailors; Titian was the great Venetian painter

explanation.surface: A great planner hands provisions to a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: TACK plus TITIAN, said quickly, sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A mastermind is a clever planner of schemes, just as a skilled strategist plans moves.

clue.text: Two animals joined the act in 1913

parts.note: a cat is one animal
and is the word that joins two things
a mouse is the other animal

explanation.surface: A pair of animals joined a stage act just before the First World War.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1913 Prisoners Act let hunger-striking suffragettes be freed and then rearrested, so it was nicknamed after a pair of animals. 'act' looks like a stage turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Its nickname was the Cat and Mouse Act, after the British law of that year on releasing and re-arresting prisoners.

clue.text: Characteristically, old military academy is in disarray

explanation.surface: The old army college is in a typical state of chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: The Shop was the nickname of the Royal Military Academy at Woolwich in London, so something typical of it throughout is cryptically 'all over' it; 'is' links.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the British idiom for scattered everywhere and chaotic; and, read literally, it means typical of every part of the Woolwich academy nicknamed The Shop.

clue.text: Being roughly sixteen, starts on college education

indicators.note: roughly means approximately or in a rough way, so the letters are jumbled
starts on points at the first letter of each following word

explanation.surface: A teenager about sixteen begins their university course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughly' rearranges SIXTEEN into EXISTEN; 'starts on' adds C and E from 'college education'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being, as a noun, is the state of being alive or real.

clue.text: Freedom to promote animal book

parts.note: lib is short for liberation, freedom

indicators.note: to promote means to raise, so in this down entry the word reads upwards

parts.note: the otter is a river animal

explanation.surface: Liberty to advertise a book about animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to promote' lifts OTTER so it reads upwards as RETTO in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The words of an opera or musical are printed as a little book.

clue.text: Switching to horse winning on personal merit

indicators.note: switching means changing places, so the letters of the following words swap around

explanation.surface: A punter changes to the horse that is winning, deservedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Switching' rearranges the fourteen letters of TO HORSE WINNING.
explanation.definitionFit: Having something by virtue of one's own qualities or claim, not through another person.

clue.text: To argue fallaciously causes offence

indicators.note: fallaciously means falsely or in a mistaken way, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Arguing with false reasoning gives offence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fallaciously' rearranges TO ARGUE; 'causes' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Indignation or a shocking wrong that provokes it.

clue.text: Shamefaced workman carrying note turned up to work

indicators.note: carrying means holding, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a hand is a manual worker
G is a musical note

indicators.note: turned up means read upwards in this down entry

parts.note: to go means to work or function

explanation.surface: An embarrassed labourer carries a message and then turns up for his shift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carrying' puts the note inside the workman; 'turned up' reverses 'to work' in this down entry. 'note' looks like a message, but it is a musical letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Looking guilty and abashed, with the cowed air of a beaten dog.

clue.text: Modest about expedition

parts.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about
expedition here means speed or haste

explanation.surface: A modest person on a journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'expedition' looks like a journey but means promptness.
explanation.definitionFit: Pure, decent and restrained in behaviour.

clue.text: Blackguard dotty about port

parts.note: a rotter is a cad or scoundrel

indicators.note: about here means turned around, so the word follows backwards

parts.note: dotty means crazy or mad

explanation.surface: A crazy villain hangs around the harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns MAD into DAM.
explanation.definitionFit: The great Dutch city at the mouth of the Rhine is one of the world's busiest harbours.

clue.text: Jugs where you will find 'atchet men?

indicators.note: 'atchet is hatchet with its opening letter dropped, the Cockney way, so the H goes from the word for the men

parts.note: hewers are men who chop with an axe, the hatchet men of the clue

explanation.surface: Where would you find men with hatchets, someone asks about pitchers?
explanation.walkthrough: Hatchet men would be HEWERS; dropping the H the Cockney way, as 'atchet does, leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Large pitchers or water jugs, as once stood in a washstand basin.

clue.text: Smell not originating in fish

indicators.note: not originating means the word loses its opening letter, where it begins

parts.note: a stench is a foul smell

explanation.surface: A smell that doesn't come from fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not originating' drops the first letter of STENCH; 'in' links.
explanation.definitionFit: A freshwater species of the carp family found in European ponds.

clue.text: Hunt down, after tailing game around

indicators.note: around here means turned round, so the shortened word is read backwards
tailing means docking the tail, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: écarté is a nineteenth-century card game for two players

explanation.surface: A hunter, having followed a quarry, circles back to track it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tailing' cuts ECARTE to ECART and 'around' reverses that; 'after' links. 'tailing' looks like following a quarry, but here it means cutting off a tail.
explanation.definitionFit: To trace someone is to track and locate them.

clue.text: Bit of meat not used or cooked

indicators.note: cooked suggests the words are tampered with or doctored, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A piece of meat that was never eaten or cooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' rearranges NOT USED OR.
explanation.definitionFit: A small round cut of beef fillet, a classic French steak.

clue.text: Attired but not oddly in attire

indicators.note: but not oddly means leaving out the odd-numbered letters and keeping the even ones

explanation.surface: Dressed, though not strangely, in clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but not oddly' keeps the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters of 'Attired'; 'in' links.
explanation.definitionFit: A necktie is an item of clothing worn with a shirt.

clue.text: Bishop is to superintend

parts.note: the Greek word behind bishop, episkopos, means one who watches over, so a bishop's role is literally to supervise

explanation.surface: A churchman's job is to supervise the diocese.
explanation.definitionFit: To superintend is to supervise or keep watch over, which is what the Greek name for a bishop says he does.

clue.text: Table-centre from the east English traveller's brought back

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for east

indicators.note: brought back means returned, so the pieces are read backwards

parts.note: a rep is a commercial traveller, a salesman

explanation.surface: A centrepiece brought home from the Orient by an English salesman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought back' reverses English plus traveller, which then follow the east; 'from' links. A rep is a commercial traveller, a salesman on the road.
explanation.definitionFit: An ornamental stand with branches holding dishes of fruit or flowers, set in the middle of a dining table.
